corrected_value.title_o: Catechol-O-methyltransferase Val158Met genotype moderates the effect of disorganized attachment on social development in young children
corrected_value.title: Catechol-O-methyltransferase Val158Met genotype moderates the effect of disorganized attachment on social development in young children
corrected_value.authors: Hygen, B. W., Guzey, I. C., Belsky, J., Berg-Nielsen, T. S., Wichstrøm, L.

decisions.quote:
It is important to appreciate that our focus on
COMT
should not be read to imply that only this polymorphism may play a moderating role vis-à-vis the effects of disorganization. Rather, we focused exclusively on this candidate gene because we conceptualized this inquiry from its inception as an attempt to test an intriguing and most original hypothesis and, thereby, conceptually replicate and extend the work of Hygen et al. (
2014
).
decisions.reason: Both the shipped record and blind coding identify Hygen et al. (2014), 'Catechol-O-methyltransferase Val158Met genotype moderates the effect of disorganized attachment on social development in young children' (DOI: 10.1017/S0954579414000492), as the sole target original study whose COMT x attachment disorganization interaction hypothesis is conceptually replicated.

Both the shipped record and blind coding classify the study as a 'replication'. The paper uses an independent US cohort (560 children from the NICHD Study of Early Child Care and Youth Development) to re-test the published COMT x attachment disorganization interaction reported in a Norwegian cohort by Hygen et al. (2014).

decisions.quote:
Nevertheless, what remains difficult to understand is why the targeted
COMT
-X-disorganization interaction only predicted change over time in the original Norwegian research and not levels of child behavior at either 4 or 6 years. Here, though, we found in our primary analyses that when disorganization was (a) measured categorically rather than continuously, (b) using the gold-standard Strange Situation rather than a story-stem completion task, and (c) at 15 months rather than at 4 years of age, that levels of kindergarten social behavior reported (only) by mothers could be accounted for by considering the moderation by
COMT
of attachment disorganization. Quite conceivably, these measurement and design differences across studies are responsible for the differences in findings across the two studies.
In any event, reasonably consistent support for the Norwegian hypothesis emerged in both inquiries as to why some children with disorganized attachment histories behave in seemingly controlling-caregiving and others in controlling-punitive ways. Especially notable, perhaps, is that in both studies the genetically-related divergent patterns of functioning are restricted to maternal reports of child behavior, thereby underscoring the relationship-specificity of disorganized attachment, at least when examined from the perspective of a gene -X-disorganization interaction.
decisions.reason: Both the shipped row and blind coding record 'successful' by treating the authors' statements of support for 'the Norwegian hypothesis' as an unqualified Rule 1 whole-original replication verdict. However, in both the Introduction and the primary/sensitivity Discussion, Li et al. (2016) explicitly distinguish Hygen et al.'s (2014) initial theoretical hypothesis from Hygen et al.'s actual empirical findings: in Hygen et al. (2014), the COMT x attachment disorganization interaction predicted only change in social behavior from age 4 to 6 and did not predict levels of child behavior at age 4 or 6, whereas Li et al. (2016) tested and found the COMT x disorganization interaction for levels of social functioning (at kindergarten and Grade 6), explicitly acknowledging 'the differences in findings across the two studies' (alongside sensitivity analyses indicating a linear 3-level gene effect rather than Hygen et al.'s nonlinear 2-level pattern). At the same time, Li et al. confirm Hygen et al.'s empirical pattern of divergent maternal-reported positive and negative behavior between disorganized Met carriers and Val/Val homozygotes, absence of genetic differences among organized children, and relationship specificity to maternal rather than teacher reports. Because agreement with an original hypothesis does not override the authors' explicit contrast between the original change-only/null-levels finding and the present levels finding, aggregating the confirmed and contrasting original-specific empirical comparisons yields 'mixed'.
